extracted.intended_audience: state and local recipients of EPA funding, EPA Office of Civil Rights staff, environmental justice advocates, community organizations, and industry/permitting stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive standards for analyzing, filing, and investigating Title VI complaints in the environmental permitting context, including recipient approaches, investigation steps, evidentiary and jurisdictional criteria, and use/limits of area-specific agreements and ADR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three general recipient approaches for Title VI issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft Recipient Guidance provides three general approaches recipients should use to analyze and resolve issues that may lead to Title VI complaints: (1) a comprehensive approach, (2) an area-specific approach, and (3) a case-by-case approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brief descriptions: the comprehensive approach integrates most Title VI activities; the area-specific approach identifies geographic areas where adverse disparate impacts may exist; the case-by-case approach allows a recipient to develop criteria to evaluate permit actions likely to raise Title VI concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive approach elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The comprehensive approach integrates all or most of the Title VI activities in the Draft Recipient Guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed activities include implementing staff training opportunities, encouraging effective public participation and outreach, conducting adverse impact and demographic analyses, encouraging intergovernmental involvement, participating in alternative dispute resolution, reducing or eliminating alleged adverse disparate impact(s), and evaluating Title VI activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area-specific agreements (purpose and content)
rubrics_metrics.description: Area-specific agreements identify geographic areas where adverse disparate health impacts or other potential Title VI concerns may exist and encourage recipients to work collaboratively with affected communities to reduce or eliminate adverse disparate impact in particular geographic areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: agreements may identify a maximum amount of pollutants for air and water that can be discharged into a certain area over a particular time period. Agreements also require recipients to continue operating their programs in compliance with the nondiscrimination requirements of Title VI and EPA's Title VI regulations. State or local agencies develop these agreements while OCR reviews them to ensure appropriate results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for OCR deference to area-specific agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: If OCR accepts a Title VI complaint relating to permitting activity covered by an area-specific agreement, it defers to the provisions in the agreement only if the agreement is supported by underlying analyses meeting specific standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deference is given only if the agreement is supported by underlying analyses that have sufficient depth, breadth, completeness, and accuracy, are relevant to the Title VI concerns, and will result in actual reductions over a reasonable time to the point of eliminating or reducing, to the extent required by Title VI, conditions that might result in a finding of non-compliance with EPA's Title VI regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: OCR actions regarding area-specific agreements (dismissal vs. investigation)
rubrics_metrics.description: OCR will close an area-specific agreement investigation if it determines the agreement eliminates or reduces an existing adverse disparate impact, but can initiate its own investigation if it determines the agreement does not produce significant reductions in environmental hazards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR can also consider other information, including complainant-provided information, and generally relies on its initial assessment and dismisses complaints against a recipient that include allegations relating to other permitting actions covered by the same agreement. Exception: complaints alleging improper implementation of the agreement or substantially changed circumstances will not be dismissed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) as a case-management tool
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA strongly supports ADR as a means of reducing Title VI administrative complaints and managing its complaint caseload; EPA views ADR as a case management tool because a complaint can be dismissed if resolved in ADR and withdrawn from the administrative process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA may negotiate with a funding recipient and request participation by other parties. OCR's responsibilities in informal proceedings include securing federal interests and preventing violations. Stakeholder concerns: ADR can exclude complainants, exacerbate bargaining-power inequities, and not guarantee fair consideration of complainant interests; formal adjudication may better equalize positions and protect rights. ADR is discussed further in Chapter 5.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complaint processing steps (Draft Revised Investigation Guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: OCR adheres to a sequence of procedural steps when processing Title VI complaints pursuant to federal standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steps listed: acknowledgement of the complaint; acceptance of the complaint for investigation, rejection, or referral; investigation; preliminary finding of noncompliance; formal finding of noncompliance; voluntary compliance; and the hearing/appeal process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six-step procedure for determining whether an adverse disparate impact exists
rubrics_metrics.description: The guidance presents a six-step procedure OCR will use to determine whether an adverse disparate impact exists in a permitting decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Six steps: assessing applicability of Title VI to the permit; defining the scope of the investigation; conducting an impact assessment; making an adverse impact decision; characterizing populations and conducting comparisons; and making an adverse disparate impact assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of existing environmental laws, regulations, policies, and scientific standards in disparity analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The Draft Revised Investigation Guidance explains how the agency will consider existing environmental laws, regulations, policies, and scientific standards to determine when health indicator levels are adverse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This expands disparity analysis concepts from prior Interim Guidance and informs how OCR evaluates whether environmental/health indicator levels qualify as harmful for Title VI purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for identifying and characterizing the affected population
rubrics_metrics.description: The guidance explains the method used to identify and determine the characteristics of the affected population for Title VI analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance provides steps and criteria for characterizing populations and selecting comparison populations as part of the adverse disparate impact analysis (see the six-step procedure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional sufficiency criteria for accepting a Title VI complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: When reviewing Title VI complaints for jurisdictional sufficiency, EPA evaluates each complaint for compliance with four criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The four criteria: whether the complaint describes the acts that allegedly violate EPA's Title VI regulations; whether the complaint identifies an EPA funding recipient as the respondent; whether the complaint is in writing; whether the complaint is filed within 180 calendar days of an alleged discriminatory activity. If criteria are absent, EPA may request supplemental information (telephonic, electronic, written, or in person) and may communicate multiple times to obtain sufficient information. EPA may also use internal resources to ascertain recipient status.

rubrics_metrics.name: 180-calendar-day filing deadline and related timeliness rules
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's implementing regulations require a complaint to be filed within 180 calendar days of the alleged discriminatory acts unless OCR waives the time limit for good cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance notes complaints alleging discriminatory effects resulting from a permit should be filed within 180 calendar days of issuance of that permit. EPA may dismiss a complaint involved in litigation or administrative appeal but may waive timeliness if complainant refiles after judicial/appellate processes are exhausted. Stakeholders dispute when the 180-day period begins (e.g., before a final/reviewable agency action) and whether the period is sufficient given the time required to develop evidence of discriminatory patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: OCR decision-timing requirement (20 calendar days)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to its regulations, OCR is required to review a Title VI complaint and either accept, reject, or refer it to the appropriate federal agency for further action within 20 calendar days of acknowledgement of the complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The report documents many instances where EPA/OCR failed to meet this 20-day requirement and the consequences for complainants and case backlog management.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Due weight' to recipient-conducted disparate impact analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: To provide state agencies an incentive for active Title VI programs, EPA assigns 'due weight' to funding recipients' adverse disparate impact investigations under certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At a minimum, recipient analyses considered for 'due weight' must reflect accepted scientific methods. However, OCR cannot entirely rely on recipient assessments—nothing precludes OCR from conducting an independent investigation or considering other relevant information. Stakeholders criticize excessive reliance on recipient analyses and urge OCR to conduct independent reviews and ensure complainants have access to resources to produce comparable analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Authority to consider' limitation on investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Draft Revised Investigation Guidance limits investigations to pollutants and impacts 'within the recipient's authority to consider' as defined under applicable state laws and regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This can allow states to narrow the types of impacts considered (e.g., socioeconomic impacts may be excluded in some states), potentially preventing Title VI adverse disparate impact claims based on categories of harm not within the recipient's state-granted authority. Civil rights advocates argue this improperly narrows federal civil rights enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of remedies and applicability of Title VI
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance indicates denial or revocation of a permit is not necessarily an appropriate remedy because a single permit is unlikely to be the sole cause of an adverse disparate impact; Title VI applicability is limited to recipients of federal financial assistance, not federal agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil rights groups contend Title VI requires recipients to consider all impacts (not solely environmental) of permitting decisions and that EPA must be prepared to terminate federal funding for recipients that discriminate (except in employment cases). EPA maintains it is not subject to Title VI's definition of 'program or activity' for federal agencies but asserts it uses Executive Order 12,898 to avoid disproportionately high and adverse impacts.
